lead: An open thin-walled section, an angle, channel, Z or stringer, has no closed loop for a shear flow to circulate round. It carries torque the way a flat strip does, with shear stress that changes sign through the thickness. Its torsion constant grows with the cube of the wall thickness, so it is very flexible in torsion. This chapter gives J = Σbt³/3, the surface stress and the rate of twist, and compares an open angle with a closed box made from the same strip.
prereq: You need: Bredt–Batho torsion of closed sections from the Bredt–Batho chapter, for the comparison.

sections.h3: Open walls twist strip by strip

blocks.text: Under a torque T, each wall of an open section behaves like a long thin rectangular strip. The shear stress runs along the wall, is zero on the mid-line and rises linearly to equal and opposite values at the two faces. The stresses on the two halves of the thickness form a couple with a lever arm of order t, which is why the stiffness is so small. Summing the strips, with the stress at the faces the same function of the rate of twist in every wall:

blocks.where: J is the torsion constant of the open section (mm⁴); b is the length of one wall along its mid-line (mm); t is that wall's thickness (mm); the sum covers every wall. The 1/3 is the long-strip value; it is accurate when b is more than about ten times t.

blocks.text: Double every thickness and J rises eight times; double every length and it only doubles. An open section also warps: its cross-section does not stay plane. The formula assumes the warping is free; where a rib or a fixed end restrains it, axial stresses appear and the member is stiffer, which needs the theory of restrained torsion.
dθ/dz = T/(G J),   θ = T L/(G J)
blocks.where: dθ/dz is the rate of twist (rad/mm); G is the shear modulus (N/mm²), about 27,000 for aluminium alloys and 79,000 for steel; L the length (mm); θ the total twist (rad).

blocks.text: τ = 2G n dθ/dz,   τ<sub>max</sub> = G t dθ/dz = T t/J
blocks.where: τ is the shear stress at a distance n from the mid-line of a wall (N/mm²); τ<sub>max</sub> is the stress at the faces of a wall of thickness t (mm). Every wall twists at the same rate, so τ<sub>max</sub> is largest in the thickest wall.

items: The largest stress is on the faces of the thickest wall, not the thinnest.
The stress is zero on the mid-line, so no constant shear flow exists: ∫τ dt across the wall is zero.
For a section built from one strip of uniform thickness, J = (total mid-line length) × t³/3, whatever its shape: an angle, a channel or a flat strip of the same length are equal in torsion.

blocks.text: Take a 2 mm strip 120 mm long. Bent into a 60 mm × 60 mm angle it has J = 120 × 2³/3 = 320 mm⁴. Bent into a 30 mm × 30 mm square tube and closed with a seam, the same strip has A = 900 mm², ∮ds/t = 120/2 = 60 and J = 4A²/∮ds/t = 54,000 mm⁴, about 170 times stiffer, from identical material. The closed tube carries the torque as a constant shear flow at a lever arm of the whole section, the open angle only across the thickness.

This is why a wing torsion box is a closed cell between the spars, and why open stringers, which are stiff in bending, are never relied on for torque. A cut that opens a closed tube, a slot, an access hole without a doubler, turns it back into an open section and destroys its torsional stiffness.

figure.caption: The first worked example: one 120 mm strip of 2 mm sheet, bent open into an angle or closed into a tube. Open, its stress changes sign across the 2 mm wall and reaches 62.5 N/mm² at the faces; closed, a uniform 2.78 N/mm² flows round the loop, and the tube is 169 times stiffer.

Right: a closed square tube 30 by 30 millimetres from the same strip, enclosing 900 square millimetres, with J equal to 54,000, stress 2.78 and twist 0.393 degrees per metre, 169 times stiffer. Below each, a sketch of stress across the wall thickness: for the angle a linear distribution from plus 62.5 to minus 62.5, zero on the mid-line; for the tube a uniform 2.78.

examples.question: A 2 mm strip 120 mm long is formed (a) into an equal angle with 60 mm legs and (b) into a closed square tube of 30 mm side. Each is 1 m long, aluminium with G = 27 GPa, and carries T = 10 N·m. Find J, the largest shear stress and the twist for each.
steps: τ<sub>max</sub> = T t/J = 10,000 × 2/320 = 62.5 N/mm², on the faces of both legs.
Ratio of stiffness: 54,000/320 = 169; ratio of stress: 62.5/2.78 = 22.5.
examples.answer: Angle: J = 320 mm⁴, τ<sub>max</sub> = 62.5 N/mm², θ = 66.3°. Tube: J = 54,000 mm⁴, τ = 2.78 N/mm², θ = 0.393°. Same strip, 169 times stiffer when closed.

examples.question: A channel stringer has two flanges 50 mm × 3 mm and a web 100 mm × 2 mm (mid-line lengths). It carries T = 15 N·m, with G = 27 GPa. Find J, the stress in the flanges and in the web, and the rate of twist.
steps: Flange faces: τ = T t/J = 15,000 × 3/1166.7 = 38.6 N/mm².
The flanges, two-thirds of the wall length, provide 77 per cent of J because of the cube of their thickness.
examples.answer: J = 1166.7 mm⁴; τ = 38.6 N/mm² in the flanges and 25.7 N/mm² in the web; 27.3° per metre.

traps: Applying Bredt–Batho to an open section. The 60 mm angle has no enclosed area; its J is 320 mm⁴.
Writing Σbt instead of Σbt³/3. The cube is the whole point.
Putting τ<sub>max</sub> in the thinnest wall. All walls twist at the same rate, so the thickest has the largest stress.
Leaving G in GPa and T in N·m. Convert both to N and mm; one slip alone makes θ 1000 times wrong.

quiz.q: Write J for a thin-walled open section and define each symbol.
quiz.a: J = Σbt³/3: b the mid-line length of each wall (mm), t its thickness (mm), J in mm⁴.

quiz.q: How does the shear stress vary through the thickness of an open wall under torque?
quiz.a: Linearly, from zero on the mid-line to equal and opposite maxima on the two faces.

quiz.q: Why is an open section so much weaker in torsion than a closed one?
quiz.a: Its stresses form a couple across the thickness t, a tiny lever arm, so J ∝ t³. A closed section carries a constant shear flow round the whole loop, at the scale of the section, so J ∝ A²t/s.

quiz.q: A flat strip 100 mm × 3 mm, 1 m long, carries T = 50 N·m with G = 27 GPa. Find J, τ<sub>max</sub> and the twist.
quiz.a: J = 100 × 27/3 = 900 mm⁴; τ<sub>max</sub> = 50,000 × 3/900 = 166.7 N/mm²; θ = 50,000 × 1000/(27,000 × 900) = 2.06 rad. This stress is beyond the elastic range of most aluminium alloys, so the elastic answer only shows how flexible the strip is.

quiz.q: Every wall of an open section is made three times thicker. How do J, τ<sub>max</sub> and the twist change for the same torque?
quiz.a: J rises 27 times; τ<sub>max</sub> = T t/J falls to 3/27 = 1/9; the twist falls to 1/27.

quiz.q: Why does a wing torque box use a closed cell while its stringers are open sections?
quiz.a: The closed cell has J = 4A²/∮ds/t, so a thin skin round a large area gives high torsional stiffness at low stress. Open stringers have J = Σbt³/3, so they would twist far too much; they are used for bending stiffness and to stabilise the skin, and the cell carries the torque.

beyond: Not for the exam. Where warping is restrained, open sections carry torque partly by bending of their flanges, described by a warping constant. Search for "Vlasov torsion" and "warping constant".
